passages.t: The Lord on his throne, and Holy, holy, holy
passages.happening:
‘In the year that King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord seated on a throne, high and exalted; and the train of His robe filled the temple’ (verse 1).

Above him stand seraphim, each with six wings. With two they cover their faces, with two their feet, and with two they fly (verse 2). They call out to one another: ‘Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of Hosts; all the earth is full of His glory’ (verse 3).

At the sound of their voices the doorposts and thresholds shake, and the temple fills with smoke (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
King Uzziah reigned over Judah for about fifty-two years and died around 740 BC; scholars' dates range from about 742 to 734. His reign was one of Judah's most prosperous. But Chronicles records that in his pride he went into the temple to burn incense, a task reserved for priests, and was struck with a skin disease that kept him apart until he died. Isaiah sees the true King in the temple in the year the proud earthly king died.

The temple's inner room held the ark beneath two golden cherubim, understood as God's footstool and throne. Isaiah sees what the temple stood for: the Lord enthroned, so vast that only the hem of his robe fills the building. Kings wore long robes as a mark of rank, and a longer train meant greater majesty.

The seraphim appear by that name only here in the Bible. The word means burning ones. They cover their faces because they cannot look on God, and they sing. The threefold holy is the Hebrew way of saying the utmost: God is utterly holy. From this vision Isaiah takes the name he uses for God through the whole book, the Holy One of Israel.

Isaiah tells his call here, in chapter 6, rather than at the start, perhaps to show where his severe message came from.
passages.later: Revelation hears the same song in heaven: “Holy, Holy, Holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come!” (Revelation 4:8). And John writes that ‘Isaiah said these things because he saw Jesus’ glory and spoke about Him’ (John 12:41).
passages.asks: Isaiah saw the true King in the year the earthly king died. Ask what has to fall in your own life before you can see who is really on the throne. And ask what it would mean for you that the whole earth, including your ordinary place in it, is full of his glory.

passages.t: Unclean lips, a burning coal, and a ready answer
passages.happening:
Isaiah cries out that he is ruined, ‘because I am a man of unclean lips dwelling among a people of unclean lips; for my eyes have seen the King, the LORD of Hosts’ (verse 5).

Then one of the seraphim flies to him with a glowing coal taken with tongs from the altar (verse 6). He touches Isaiah's mouth with it and says, ‘Now that this has touched your lips, your iniquity is removed and your sin is atoned for’ (verse 7).

Then Isaiah hears the voice of the Lord: ‘Whom shall I send? Who will go for Us?’ (verse 8). And he answers, “Here am I. Send me!” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
In Israel's worship, unclean lips were a serious matter. Uncleanness barred a person from God's presence, and Isaiah has seen the King. His cry is not false modesty. He knows he cannot stand there.

The altar is probably the incense altar that stood before the inner room. The verb for atone, kaphar, is the verb used for the sacrifices of Leviticus and the Day of Atonement. Isaiah's cleansing comes from God's side, from the altar. He does nothing but receive it.

Only after he is cleansed does the question come. The scene is a heavenly council, as when the prophet Micaiah saw the LORD on his throne with the host of heaven around him. Isaiah's call follows a pattern found also in the calls of Moses, Gideon, Jeremiah and Ezekiel: an encounter with God, a sense of unworthiness, reassurance and a commission. Isaiah's answer is the shortest and readiest of them all.
passages.later: Jeremiah answered his call very differently: ‘I surely do not know how to speak, for I am only a child’ (Jeremiah 1:6). And when Simon Peter saw who Jesus was, he fell at his knees and begged him to go away, ‘for I am a sinful man’ (Luke 5:8).
passages.asks: Isaiah was sent only after he was cleansed. Ask whether you have been trying to serve God before letting him deal with your sin. And ask what it would take for you to answer as Isaiah did, and mean it.

passages.t: A hard commission, and a holy stump
passages.happening:
The commission is hard. Isaiah is to tell the people to go on ‘ever hearing, but never understanding; be ever seeing, but never perceiving’ (verse 9). ‘Make the hearts of this people calloused; deafen their ears and close their eyes. Otherwise they might see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their hearts, and turn and be healed’ (verse 10).

Isaiah asks, ‘How long, O Lord?’ (verse 11). The answer: until the cities lie ruined and empty, the houses deserted, the land desolate, and the LORD has driven people far away (verses 11-12).

‘And though a tenth remains in the land, it will be burned again. As the terebinth and oak leave stumps when felled, so the holy seed will be a stump in the land’ (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
The commission is built as a mirrored pattern: heart, ears, eyes, then eyes, ears, heart. Isaiah is told that his preaching will harden the people rather than heal them.

The first hearers had already refused God's word again and again, as chapters 1 to 5 show. Within a few years Judah would face invasion from Aram and Israel, and within twenty years the northern kingdom would be destroyed. The desolation of verses 11 to 13 unfolded over the next century and a half, ending with Babylon's destruction of Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC.

But the chapter does not end in despair. A tree that is cut down leaves a stump, and a stump can sprout. The holy seed is the stump. The book will soon speak of a shoot from the stump of Jesse.
passages.later: Jesus quoted these verses to explain why many did not understand his parables (Matthew 13:14-15), and Paul quoted them in Rome (Acts 28:26-27). Paul also wrote, ‘A hardening in part has come to Israel, until the full number of the Gentiles has come in’ (Romans 11:25), and went on, ‘And so all Israel will be saved’ (Romans 11:26).
passages.hard:
Why would God send a prophet to make hearts dull so that people would not turn and be healed?

These are among the hardest words in the prophets. Many interpreters read the commands as describing the result of Isaiah's preaching rather than its purpose: his faithful message would harden people who had already refused God, as the same sun that melts wax hardens clay. Others stress that this is a judicial hardening, a judgment on those who had long resisted, not a hardening of the innocent. In Exodus, Pharaoh's hardening is described both as his own act and as God's.

The hardening is also limited. Isaiah asks how long, and the answer implies an end, and the chapter closes with a holy seed. The New Testament uses the passage to explain unbelief while still preaching and inviting, and Paul argues that Israel's hardening is partial and temporary (Romans 11:25-26). The passage does not remove the mystery of how God's rule and human responsibility meet.

These words were spoken to Isaiah's own people in his own day. They are not a label for any people now, and they are never a reason to blame the Jewish people. Paul, quoting them, insists that God has not rejected his people.
passages.asks: Isaiah was sent to preach to people who would not listen, and he went. Ask whether you would keep speaking the truth if you knew most would not hear. And ask whether there is a word from God you have heard so often that it no longer reaches you.
